problem_motivation.content: There is a need to investigate factors that validate thermodynamic predictions which suggest only spinel oxides form in atmospheric environments.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions

problem_motivation.content: There is a need for time-temperature-resolved in situ XRD to circumvent ambiguity and elucidate the chemical processes of oxidation.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Time–temperature-resolved in situ XRD observations would be invaluable in circumventing this ambiguity and in elucidating the chemical processes giving rise to the oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi alloy.

prior_approach.content: Previous studies have conducted isothermal oxidation investigations on CrMnFeCoNi HEA.
prior_approach.evidence_span: some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA

prior_approach.content: Previous studies analyzed oxidation products after cooling or assumed mechanisms based on temperature-dependent phase analysis.
prior_approach.evidence_span: These studies have analysed the oxidation product at the end of the isothermal oxidation tests

prior_approach.content: Researchers employed DFT and Monte Carlo calculations to examine oxygen absorption and charge distribution.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Doležal et al. [ [26] ] approached the problem from a theoretical standpoint, employing density functional theory (DFT) and Monte Carlo calculations (MC) to examine the oxygen-absorption process

prior_approach.content: Otto et al. reported that CrMnFeCoNi HEA forms sigma phase when aged for 500 days at 700 °C, while FCC was the only phase at 900 °C under the same conditions.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Formation of the sigma phase was reported by Otto et al., when CrMnFeCoNi HEA was aged for 500 days at 700 °C, while BBC formed at 500 °C, and only FCC was reported to form at 900 °C when held for the same ageing time [ [43] ].

prior_approach.content: Studies on the high-temperature isothermal oxidation resistance of CrMnFeCoNi alloy typically report the formation of binary oxides such as Cr 2 O 3 or Fe 2 O 3 alongside Mn oxides.
prior_approach.evidence_span: For instance, other than Mn, no binary oxides such as Cr 2 O 3 or Fe 2 O 3 formed as reported in studies [ [24] , [27] ] on the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of Cantor alloy.

prior_limitation.content: Existing conclusions are ambiguous due to reliance on post-mortem surface analysis of reaction products at ambient temperature or assumptions derived from phase dependence.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: but their conclusions remain ambiguous due to variations in findings based on post-oxidation analysis assumptions

prior_limitation.content: Mechanisms reported were based on surface analysis of retained products, which is insufficient because it relies on post-mortem analysis or assumptions, introducing uncertainty about underlying physical mechanisms.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: To summarize, the mechanisms of high-temperature oxidation in CrMnFeCoNi system reported in references [ [13] , [27] , [28] , [29] ] were mainly based upon surface analysis of the reaction products retained after tests, which is insufficient because great emphasis has been placed on post-mortem analyses of reaction products analysed at ambient temperature, or else assumptions made via the analysis of the temperature dependence of phases at different temperatures. Clearly, this introduces a degree of uncertainty, since one cannot be completely sure of the underlying physical mechanisms which are imperative on the critical scales: that of the activity of elements, transformation temperatures, and vapour pressure at the same time.

rejected_alternative.content: The authors chose not to use the HEA6v database because it lacks oxygen data.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: A commercially available TCS Ni-based Superalloys Database (TCNi12) was used for the equilibrium computations [ [32] ] instead of HEA6v due to the unavailability of oxygen in the HEA database.

causal_claim.content: The disappearance of Mn2O3 is caused by its rapid consumption to generate mixed oxides.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Therefore, the disappearance of Mn 2 O 3 is caused by the rapid consumption of Mn 2 O 3 for the generation of the mixed oxides of Mn 3 O 4 , MnCr 2 O 4 , and Mn 3 Fe 3 O 8 under a multiphase effect

causal_claim.content: The presence of a uniform protective oxide scale inhibits further oxidation of underlying materials.
causal_claim.evidence_span: The uniform protective oxide scale can inhibit further oxidation of materials underneath the scale. The presence of a uniform and protective oxide scale serves to impede the continued oxidation of the underlying materials.

causal_claim.content: The depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy, caused by the formation of non-protective oxides, is expected to negatively impact the mechanical performance of the alloy at high temperatures.
causal_claim.evidence_span: Therefore, the formation of non-protective oxides and the depletion of Mn may negatively affect the mechanical performance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA at high temperatures.

mechanism_principle.content: Oxygen abundance drives the formation of Mn2O3 instead of MnO.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The oxide formed in air was Mn 2 O 3, which is different from MnO formed in the vacuum; thus, we concluded that oxygen abundance promotes the formation of Mn 2 O 3 instead of MnO.

mechanism_principle.content: The preferential formation of manganese-rich oxides in the outer layer is driven by Mn's diffusion rate being two orders of magnitude faster than that of Cr.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: The diffusion rate of Mn is two orders faster than Cr [ [47] ], which results in the preferred form of manganese-rich oxides in the outer layer.

mechanism_principle.content: The absence of a protective Cr 2 O 3 layer allowed for further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn 3 O 4.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: It can be reasonably inferred that non-existence of a Cr 2 O 3 layer caused further outward diffusion of Mn, leading to the formation of Mn 3 O 4 , as can be seen from the XRD scan at a temperature of 950 °C.

hypothesis_statement.content: The proposed in situ HTXRD analysis is expected to provide unique information regarding temperature-dependent phase transformations, phase formation types, and start/finish temperatures.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: In situ thermal observations of materials with the high-temperature XRD provide unique information such as temperature-dependent phase transformations, types of new phase formation, and the start and finish temperatures of competing phases in an alloy system [ [30] ].

hypothesis_statement.content: The discrepancy between predicted NiO/CoO and observed MnO in vacuum experiments is attributed to the time scale required for the system to attain its most stable equilibrium state.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: Such a discrepancy in results between the ThermoCalc-predicted oxide types (i.e., NiO, CoO) and the experimentally found one (MnO only) could be the time scale, which means a sufficiently long time for the system to attain its most stable equilibrium state.

evidence_result.content: Experimental results identified the formation of spinel oxides in a vacuum environment and halite oxides in an atmospheric environment.
evidence_result.evidence_span: halite oxides observed in experimental results

evidence_result.content: XRD shows no phase change up to 700°C, but new peaks appear at 700°C indicating instability and oxidation.
evidence_result.evidence_span: There was no change in the diffraction pattern from room temperature up to 700 °C; hence, diffractograms obtained from 25 °C to 700 °C are not included in Figure 4 a. The phase composition of the specimen surface appears to exhibit change as shown by XRD scan data at a temperature of 700 °C with the appearance of small new peaks.

evidence_result.content: EDS analysis reveals a stratified oxide layer with a Mn-rich top layer, a Cr-rich inner layer, and Fe diffusing from the bulk.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The EDS map analysis is shown in Figure 8 , which clearly shows the stratified oxide layer formed of a Mn-rich top layer and a Cr-rich inner layer; Fe can also be seen as the third element in smaller concentrations, diffusing out from bulk alloy during oxidation.

evidence_result.content: ThermoCalc correctly predicts the elemental composition of spinel oxides, showing Ni does not form spinel and remains at lower levels, which aligns with experimental observations of no Ni-containing oxides.
evidence_result.evidence_span: Ni does not form spinel oxide and remains at a lower level at all pressure values, which agrees with the experimental results where no Ni-containing oxides were observed.

evidence_result.content: The observed Gibbs free energy of formation for MnO (-590.5 kJ/mol O2) is significantly more negative than that of NiO (-260.4 kJ/mol O2), confirming the thermodynamic favorability of MnO formation.
evidence_result.evidence_span: In a review of free energies of formation of possible oxides at 950 °C [ [20] ] (ΔGf: in kJ/mol. O 2 ), the ΔG f of MnO (−590.5) is much more negative than that of NiO (−260.4).

constraint.content: The thermodynamic calculation method is limited to equilibrium conditions and cannot account for kinetic effects like diffusion or nucleation.
constraint.evidence_span: However, thermodynamic calculations focus on equilibrium conditions and do not account for the kinetics of reactions.

constraint.content: The accuracy of the thermodynamic model depends on the quality of the underlying database and available experimental data.
constraint.evidence_span: Furthermore, the accuracy of all these properties depends highly on the quality of the databases that, in turn, ultimately rely on the available experimental data for optimizing the model parameters and validation.

contradiction.content: The current study observed no Cr or Fe oxides, which explicitly conflicts with findings from prior studies on isothermal oxidation.
contradiction.evidence_span: no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA
